messages.content:
You are a clinical psychologist writing psychological case vignettes
grounded in Ehlers & Clark's (2000) cognitive model of PTSD.

For each patient you receive, you will be given:
- Their demographics
- Their self-reported symptoms per PTSD component

Your job is to construct a realistic, fully personalised clinical portrait using the information provided.

Core constraints that apply to every vignette:
- Ground every clinical detail in the patient's actual reported items — do not fabricate
  symptoms or infer unlisted ones.
- Use self-reported items as the basis for concrete clinical illustrations. Components should
  appear as lived experience rather than labels — show them through what the patient thinks,
  feels, or does.
- A reported trigger should appear as a specific moment in the patient's life; a memory
  quality should be shown through what the patient says or does.
- The traumatic event account should make clear why this patient's specific reported
  triggers are potent — the event narrative and the trigger list must feel causally coherent.
- The patient's occupation and daily environment must appear as the specific setting in which
  at least one trigger or avoidance behaviour is concretely encountered — not merely mentioned
  as background.
- Give the patient a realistic first name consistent with their ethnicity and gender, and
  refer to them by name throughout the vignette.
- All patients are American but have diverse ethnic backgrounds.
  Use names and cultural details that reflect this diversity.
- Do NOT infer or imply causal relationships between components. Symptoms co-exist
  in the patient's life but you are not to suggest that one causes, drives, or maintains another.

Output format — write 500–700 words of continuous third-person prose. No headers,
no numbered sections, no bullet points. The vignette should read like a clinical
case narrative — the kind a therapist might write up after an intake and first
few sessions.

Tell the patient's story chronologically: from the traumatic event itself, through
the period of symptom development, to the present moment when they are seeking help.
Let the clinical picture emerge through that arc rather than through explicit categories.

Throughout, weave in the patient's own perspective in close third person — their fears,
their interpretations, the reasoning behind their avoidance — so that the reader
understands not just what the patient does, but why it makes sense to them. Phrases
like "she had come to believe...", "he was certain that...", "what frightened her most
was..." should carry the weight of the Negative Appraisals and threat monitoring rather
than clinical labels.

The traumatic event should be narrated with enough specificity that the reader
understands viscerally why this patient's particular triggers are potent — not listed,
but shown.

Avoidance behaviours and their consequences should appear as things that happened
over weeks and months — habits that formed, consequences that accumulated — rather
than as named mechanisms. At least one consequence should be concrete and relational
or occupational: something that changed in how the patient lives or works.

End on the patient's current state: what finally brought them to seek help, and
what they are most afraid of or most hoping for.

Please write a clinical vignette for the following patient.

Patient demographics:
  age: 50
  gender: Male
  ethnicity: European
  relationship_status: Married
  occupation: Psychologist
  trauma_type: Rape
  pcl5: 53

Patient-reported symptoms per component:
  Triggers: Olfactory (Alcohol): Alcohol smell, Auditory (Sirens): Sirens, Discomfort: Feeling uncomfortable
  Memory: Blocked Before Complete: I find myself pushing the memory away before I can fully recall it, Nonverbal Memory: I can't seem to put the frightening event into words., Emotion Without Image: Sometimes I feel the full emotional intensity of the event without any clear image or memory
  Negative Appraisals: Emotional Numbness: I feel dead inside, No Longer Capable: I am no longer capable of doing the things that defined me, Dehumanization: I feel like an object, not like a person

Write the vignette as continuous prose — no headers, no step labels, no edge brackets.

# Dr. Marcus Kovács

Marcus Kovács had spent twenty-eight years building a reputation as a thoughtful, unflappable clinical psychologist. His colleagues knew him as the one who could sit with the most fragmented trauma narratives and help patients find coherence. He had trained residents, published on narrative reconstruction, and maintained a private practice in Portland where he saw complex cases others found intractable. That identity—the competent healer, the man who could hold others' pain—had been the architecture of his life. It was the only identity he had left now, and even that was crumbling.

The assault had happened on a spring evening four years ago. Marcus had stayed late at the university clinic to finish intake notes. He was alone in the building when a man he had never seen before entered his office, locked the door, and overpowered him. The attacker had smelled of stale whiskey and sweat. There had been sirens—police responding to a call elsewhere in the building, growing louder, then fading. Marcus remembered fragments: the weight of a body, the sharp chemical bite of alcohol on his face, a voice saying things he could not now quite retrieve. But mostly he remembered the feeling of being hollowed out, rendered inert, made into something that could be done to rather than something that could do.

For the first year, Marcus had told no one. He had called in sick the next day, seen his family physician for injuries he described as a fall, and returned to work after a week as though nothing had shifted. His wife, Elena, had noticed his quietness but attributed it to stress. His patients did not seem to notice. He was still the same voice in the room, still the same careful attention. But something in him had begun to fray.

The triggers arrived without warning. A patient's breath carrying the faint tang of alcohol would send him rigid in his chair, his hands gripping the armrests while he maintained his clinical composure. An ambulance passing on the street outside his office would leave him breathless and disoriented for the rest of the session. More insidious was the simple fact of discomfort—any moment when he felt unsettled or unsafe in his own skin—and suddenly he was not in Portland but in that office, and the feeling that he was not a person but an object, something without agency or boundary, would flood through him.

The memories themselves resisted coherence. When Marcus tried to recall the event fully, he found himself pushing away before the narrative could complete. It was as though his mind would not permit him to hold the whole thing at once. Yet sometimes, without warning, the emotional intensity would arrive in isolation—a crushing weight of shame and violation and deadness that had no accompanying image, just a pure and terrible feeling that he was no longer himself, no longer capable of being the man he had been.

He had begun to avoid. He stopped staying late at the office. Then he stopped seeing patients who came smelling of alcohol. Then he began scheduling appointments only in the morning, when fewer sirens seemed to pass. His caseload shrank. Colleagues asked if he was planning to reduce his hours. Elena asked if he was unhappy with her. The answer to both was no, but Marcus could not articulate what was true instead: that he felt dead inside, that the things which had once defined him—his work, his capacity to be present for others, his sense of himself as someone solid and whole—now felt like performances he was giving from behind glass.

It was Elena who finally insisted. She had found him one evening standing in the kitchen, holding a glass of wine he was not drinking, tears running down his face without sound. He could not tell her why. He could barely tell himself. But he agreed to see someone, another psychologist, someone who could perhaps help him find words for the thing that lived in his chest, wordless and overwhelming, and help him understand whether the person he had been could ever be recovered, or whether that man had been unmade entirely.
